extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary students, and readers/defenders of poetry (educated Elizabethan-era audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A poetics/defense of poetry describing what poesy is, its kinds, its moral and pedagogic functions, and stylistic standards for good poetic practice. Intended as instructive guidance for evaluating and composing poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poesy as imitation (mimesis) with the end to teach and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poesy ... is an art of imitation; for so Aristotle termeth it in the word μίμησις; that is to say, a representing, counterfeiting, or figuring forth: to speak metaphorically, a speaking picture, with this end, to teach and delight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or produce poetry by its capacity to imitate (represent) in order both to instruct (teach) and to please (delight). A good poem balances these aims; the teaching should be persuasive because it is pleasurable, not merely didactic or dry. Anti-patterns: writing that is only precept (philosophical tract) or only ornament (empty prettiness) without moving the reader toward knowledge or virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general kinds of poesy (divine, philosophical/didactic, and true inventive poets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney divides poesy into three kinds: (1) chief/divine (imitating God — e.g., the Psalms); (2) poetic treatment of philosophical subjects (moral, natural, astronomical, historical); (3) the third kind — true poets who freely invent what may be and should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing, recognize the category: divine/psalmic poetry is reverent and ecclesial; didactic poetry instructs on specific disciplines; the highest poets freely invent exemplary images and actions that teach and delight. Each kind has legitimacy and different goals. Misjudging the kind (e.g., condemning didactic verse as not 'poetry') is an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's moral/pedagogic superiority: teaches by example and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet combines the strengths of the moral philosopher (precept) and the historian (example), teaching virtue not merely by abstract precepts but by making examples that move men to act: poetry 'delighteth to move men to take that goodness in hand'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem successfully instructs by providing vivid, exemplary imitation that motivates virtuous action. Prefer works that show consequences, passions, and exempla over abstract moralizing. Anti-patterns: abstract ethical treatises lacking lively exemplification; histories that only catalog facts without eliciting moral insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker (originality and creation beyond nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek term ποιητὴν (poietes) means 'to make'; the poet 'maketh' — not confined to copying nature but able to make things 'better than nature' or entirely new (heroes, chimeras, ideal characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value imaginative creation and typifying invention: the poet should generate memorable ideals and models (Cyrus, Æneas, Orlando) that readers can learn from. Anti-pattern: mere transcription of facts or slavish copying of nature without imaginative elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse is ornament; versification is not the essence of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney: versifying (rhyming/metrical dress) is apparel, not the cause of poetry; there have been excellent poets in prose (e.g., Xenophon, Heliodorus) and many versifiers who are not poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the poem by its inventive, imitative power and its capacity to teach and delight rather than by mere metrical skill. A poet may write in prose or verse; meter should be assessed as a fitting ornament to matter, not as proof of poetic worth. Anti-pattern: assuming formal verse automatically equals 'poetry'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit of manner to subject: measured diction and proportion according to dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should 'piece each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject' — i.e., adopt a style, rhythm, and diction commensurate with the subject's gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate style for appropriateness: grand subjects require proportionate language and structure; trivial subjects should not be clothed in overblown diction. Avoid mismatches of tone and subject. Good practice: carefully select words and cadences that suit the subject's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's utility as the first light-giver and primer of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry historically has introduced nations to learning (Homer, Hesiod, Dante, Chaucer); it 'draw[s] wild untamed wits to an admiration of knowledge' and serves as nursery for more complex studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a poem's civic and educational effect: does it cultivate appetite for further learning and sharpen faculties? Recognize poetry's role in early moral and intellectual formation. Anti-patterns: dismissing poetry as merely frivolous entertainment and ignoring its formative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry may rightly be used in religious/devotional contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney argues that divine scripture parts (e.g., David's Psalms) are poetical and that poetry's devices (prosopopoeia, musical instruments, personification of the divine) can be rightly applied in worship and consolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude poetry from religious use; evaluate devotional verse for reverence, suitability, and its capacity to comfort and raise the mind. Anti-pattern: Puritan-style blanket condemnation of all poetic forms as profane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres and special denominations as evaluative categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are subdivided: heroic, lyric, tragic, comic, satyric, iambic, elegiac, pastoral, etc.; some labeled by subject matter, others by verse form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genre-appropriate criteria when evaluating: judge a pastoral by pastoral conventions, an epic by heroic standards, a lyric by intenseness and musicality. Recognize that different genres require different balances of invention, ornament, and moral aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative restraint: invention must be 'reined with learned discretion'
rubrics_metrics.description: The third sort of poet 'range only, reined with learned discretion, into the divine consideration of what may be, and should be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage inventive freedom tempered by judgment and knowledge: invention should serve moral and instructive ends, not merely caprice. Anti-patterns: fanciful extravagance without ethical or intellectual grounding; deceitful or irresponsible representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poetic devices (description, prosopopoeia, passionate painting) to move readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney points to prosopopoeias, passionate descriptions (e.g., Gyges's Ring), depiction of meetings, banquets, and scenes as 'flowers of poetry' that enrich the philosophical or narrative body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a poem for effective deployment of personification, vivid scene-painting, and rhetorical devices that enliven argument or story. Devices should enhance the teaching and delighting functions rather than distract. Anti-pattern: ornament that obstructs clarity or moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's capacity to represent passions and particulars beyond historiography
rubrics_metrics.description: Historians borrow poetry's passionate descriptions and put speeches in mouths they never used; poetry's representation of passion and particularities reaches where bare history cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poets' rendering of inner life and emotion as a mode of knowledge—judge whether a poem renders passions plausibly and instructively. Beware histories that claim moral teaching but lack the vividness that moves readers to moral insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style should avoid captious or self-interested criticism and aim at highest ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney praises criticism that looks toward the end of good literature and criticizes captious, engaged, or self-seeking criticism; likewise he praises poetic style that is 'clear, direct, and manly' and not 'euphuistic extravagance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating, favor clarity, directness, and concern for moral/educational ends over ostentatious verbal display or criticism that promotes the critic's ego. Anti-patterns: euphuism (mere conceit), captious nitpicking, and self-aggrandizing commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate poetry by its works and parts (impact and components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney proposes to 'weight this latter sort of poetry by his works, and then by his parts' — i.e., judge both overall effects (works) and the constituent parts (style, invention, ornament, structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a twofold evaluation: (a) the work's overall moral and aesthetic impact (does it teach and delight? does it form virtue?), and (b) the parts (imagination, diction, figures, plot, character, meter) for technical soundness and appropriateness. Both macro and micro assessments inform judgment.
